displayQuote: Happiness is when what you think, what you say, and what you do are in harmony

meta.title: Who really said "Happiness is when what you think, what you say, and what you do are in harmony"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Everyone credits Gandhi, but no primary source pins this exact line. It echoes his real teaching on harmony of thought, word and deed — but reads as a modern paraphrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Happiness is when what you think, what you say, and what you do are in harmony'?
meta.ogDescription: Universally attributed to Gandhi, yet unsourced. Goodreads tags it 'attributed-no-source' and it is absent from Wikiquote. An honest amber verdict.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Gandhi and consistent with his widely attributed teaching to “aim at complete harmony of thought and word and deed,” but no primary source — no volume of the Collected Works, Young India, Harijan, letter or speech — pins this exact wording, which reads as a later paraphrase.

docMeta.dd: “Happiness is when what you think, what you say, and what you do are in harmony.”
“Always aim at complete harmony of thought and word and deed.”

source.excerpt: Always aim at complete harmony of thought and word and deed. Always aim at purifying your thoughts and everything will be well.
trail: The exact sentence is absent from Wikiquote’s Gandhi page ↗, which lists sourced, disputed and misattributed quotes alike.
On Goodreads the line carries the community tag “attributed-no-source” ↗.
A far more widely attributed Gandhi formulation — “Always aim at complete harmony of thought and word and deed” ↗ — shows the authentic idea the popular version compresses.
source.cutTag: ↑ the better-attributed Gandhi line is about aiming for harmony — not a definition of happiness
source.excerptNote: This harmony formulation is far more consistently attributed to Gandhi and expresses the same idea — though we have not pinned it to a specific dated Gandhi text either, so we present it as the better-established parallel, not a fully sourced citation. The famous “Happiness is when…” line is a snappier reformulation of the same thought that no editor has been able to source to Gandhi’s own words.
source.rightsNote: Gandhi’s own writings are long out of copyright, but because this specific wording cannot be traced to any dated Gandhi text its provenance — and therefore its rights status — is genuinely unknown. Treat it as an unsourced modern phrasing.

author.name: Mahatma Gandhi
author.heading: About Mahatma Gandhi
author.bio: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1869–1948), called Mahatma (‘great-souled’), led India’s independence movement through satyagraha — nonviolent civil resistance. Across his voluminous writings in Young India and Harijan he returned often to the unity of thought, word and deed as the foundation of an ethical life, which is why this popular line rings true even though its exact wording cannot be traced to him.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented as an attributed, unsourced Gandhi quote in online quotation collections; no primary Gandhi text (Collected Works, Young India, Harijan, letters) has been located containing this exact wording. The closest and far more widely attributed parallel is Mahatma Gandhi, “Always aim at complete harmony of thought and word and deed.”

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: The issue here is not a rival author — it is false precision. The line is presented everywhere as a documented Gandhi quote when no source exists for it.

items.scope: Presented as a sourced quote by
items.why: BrainyQuote, Goodreads, AZ Quotes and countless graphics stamp it “— Mahatma Gandhi” with no citation; Goodreads’ own metadata tags it “attributed-no-source” ↗, and it is missing entirely from Wikiquote’s Gandhi page ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The safest honest statement: the idea is authentically Gandhian — the widely attributed “aim at complete harmony of thought and word and deed” ↗ expresses it — but this exact happiness-themed sentence has no located primary source and should be labelled “attributed,” not quoted as verified.

context.heading: Why it rings true
lead: Gandhi is among the most-misquoted figures on the internet, which makes even his plausible lines worth checking. Fabricated or heavily-paraphrased “Gandhi” quotes — famously “Be the change you wish to see in the world” — spread precisely because they distill something he really believed into a cleaner slogan than he ever wrote.

This line follows that pattern. Gandhi genuinely and repeatedly taught that a good life requires alignment of thought, word and deed; the “Happiness is when…” formulation packages that teaching as a definition of happiness he is not documented to have made.
detailsBody: The alignment of thought, speech and action is an old ideal in Indian thought — the Sanskrit formula manasā vācā karmaṇā (‘in thought, word and deed’). Gandhi drew on that tradition, so the sentiment predates him; this is one reason the quote feels timeless and why tracing it to a single Gandhi text is so difficult.
